title: Citigroup: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors
detail:
Citigroup: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors
The Motley Fool Team, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 12:20 PM CDT 3 min read
C
Trade C on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 13, 2026, Citigroup (NYSE:C) reported net income of $5.2 billion. The bank's continuing structural overhaul cuts corporate overhead expenses to fund artificial intelligence upgrades and expand high-return corporate services. Three takeaways from management's comments stand out for long-term investors.

1. Severance Charges Fund Structural Cost Reductions and Technology

Management is trimming headcount across corporate functions to eliminate redundant expenses. Reinvesting those severance savings, which are job-termination payouts to outgoing staff, into modern technology platforms creates operational capacity for future business growth.

On a year to date basis, we have recognized over $1 billion of severance, largely across functions, technology and operations as we continue to drive structural efficiencies and bring down transformation expenses and stranded costs to create capacity for business growth.
-- Gonzalo Luchetti, Chief Financial Officer

2. Artificial Intelligence Tools Actively Reduce Software Vendor Expenses

Internal deployment of automated coding software helps engineering teams to complete technical projects in-house rather than outsourcing work. That shift lowers external software supplier costs while accelerating product rollouts for corporate clients.

We have reduced our tech vendor spend by 30% year over year as a consequence, and that is still got a long way to run.
-- Jane Nind Fraser, Chair and Chief Executive Officer

3. Asset Inflows Accelerate Fee Growth Across Wealth Management

Net new investment assets, which represent fresh capital brought in by wealth clients, doubled year over year. There was also strong uptake among retail clients who transitioned to wealth products. Expanding client accounts builds steady fee streams that protect profitability against fluctuating interest rates.

We brought in $38 billion in net new investment assets this quarter, up over 100% from a year ago.
-- Jane Nind Fraser, Chair and Chief Executive Officer

Looking Ahead

Third-quarter revenue expanded 8% year over year as execution gained traction across global services and consumer cards segments. A global institutional network, blockchain and payment tokenization for digital assets growing to seven markets, and automated risk systems build operational scale. Management is watching trading seasonality, deposit competition, and capital regulation changes.

Our strategy is working, and we have a clear path to delivering higher, sustainable returns.
-- Gonzalo Luchetti, Chief Financial Officer

The fair value estimate for Leidos Holdings has been cut slightly from US$157.73 to US$151.73 per share, a reduction of about 3.8%. This shift aligns with recent analyst debates that weigh stronger contributions from defense, intelligence, digital, and homeland work against a more challenging environment for the Health segment and its impact on valuation support. As you read on, you will see how this evolving narrative may influence the way you track Leidos Holdings from here.

Analyst Price Targets don't always capture the full story. Head over to our Company Report to find new ways to value Leidos Holdings.

What Wall Street Has Been Saying
🐂 Bullish Takeaways

Several firms still see balanced risk and reward in Leidos Holdings. RBC Capital keeps an Outperform rating with a US$170 target, while Wells Fargo keeps Equal Weight with a higher target of US$165. This reflects confidence in execution across defense and homeland focused work.

Citi and BofA both highlight solid contributions from defense, intelligence, digital, and homeland portfolios. Citi previously lifted its target to US$161 and BofA to US$135, pointing to prior Q2 strength in these areas even as they factor in ongoing Health headwinds.

🐻 Bearish Takeaways

The recent tone has turned more cautious. JPMorgan downgraded Leidos to Neutral and cut its target to US$142 from US$160, citing a tougher setup for the stock and potential downside risk to current consensus expectations.

Jefferies, TD Cowen, Goldman Sachs, and Citi have all trimmed targets in recent months, with Health segment revenue and margin uncertainty a recurring theme. Jefferies now models lower 2027 Health revenue, while Goldman Sachs and BofA point to ongoing Health pressure that could limit earnings support for the current valuation.

Citigroup reported third quarter 2026 net interest income of US$16,982 million and net income of US$5,245 million, alongside multiple new senior unsecured fixed rate note issuances across maturities from 2028 to 2049 completed on October 14, 2026.

The combination of higher reported profitability in services and wealth management and fresh long dated funding through fixed income offerings indicates that Citigroup is aligning its balance sheet with areas where the business is currently generating stronger earnings.

The next area of attention is how Citigroup's strong third quarter earnings performance could influence the broader investment narrative that investors are using.

Scan how Citigroup's latest earnings and funding moves compare with other large financial institutions by reviewing a curated set of list of solid balance sheet and fundamentals (25 results) in similar sectors.

Citigroup Investment Narrative Recap

To own Citigroup, you need to believe the current mix of Services, Markets, U.S. Personal Banking and Wealth can keep turning strong reported net interest income and net income into consistently better returns, without fresh regulatory setbacks. The recent third quarter beat shows that cost control and segment mix are working right now rather than just on paper.

The near term story hinges on execution in services, digital payments and AI automation, plus clean delivery on asset sales like Banamex and the capital return plan. The biggest risk today is operational or conduct slippage that drives new fines or higher compliance costs, which could blunt the benefit of these earnings gains.

The most relevant update alongside the earnings is Citigroup's string of new senior unsecured fixed rate notes, including US$108.454 million of 7.00% notes due 2049 and several smaller issues maturing between 2028 and 2041. This is relatively modest compared with a market value of more than US$200 billion, so the headline impact on the equity story is limited.

Even if the size is not huge, these long dated, fixed rate bonds matter for an investor tracking catalysts. They show how the bank is shaping its funding profile while capital is being freed up from divestitures and returned through buybacks and dividends. The risk is that higher cost term funding tightens the spread between what Citigroup earns on assets and what it pays on liabilities.

What Analysts Are Building Into The Citigroup Story

Citigroup's narrative projects US$108.8b revenue and US$22.4b earnings by 2029. This assumes 9.3% yearly revenue growth and an earnings increase of about US$4.5b from US$17.9b today.

Investing.com -- Shares of Johnson Matthey rose over 2% on Friday as Citi renewed coverage with a "buy" rating, saying the sale of its Catalyst Technologies business and the purchase of Cormetech set up the company for earnings growth and cash returns.

Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »

Citi set a target price of £28.50, against a share price of £24.62 at the Oct. 15 close. The bank had suspended its rating on the stock for a period. It expects a 15.8% share price gain and a 3% dividend yield, for a total return of 18.8% over 12 months.

For the year to March 2027, Citi forecasts earnings before interest and tax will rise 16%. It expects adjusted earnings per share to jump about 40% to 182 pence, helped by planned share buybacks that cut the number of shares in issue. That is 12% above analysts' consensus, Citi said.

Johnson Matthey sold Catalyst Technologies and bought Cormetech, a U.S. maker of catalysts that clean exhaust from power plants and other industrial sites, for an upfront value of $360 million, with up to $100 million more payable depending on performance.

Citi expects Cormetech's operating profit contribution to rise from about £13 million in the year to March 2027 to about £30 million the following year, citing data centre growth as one driver of power generation investment.

The company returned £1 billion from the Catalyst Technologies sale through an £800 million special dividend and a £200 million buyback.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

It has committed to return at least £200 million a year through dividends and buybacks from the year to March 2027, which Citi said equals a yield of about 6%.

Citi forecasts free cash flow will rise by about £120 million in the year to March 2028 as spending on a new UK platinum group metals refinery falls.

Citi said the current share price assumes cash returns to shareholders will fall by about 4% a year after its 10-year forecast period, with the business valued at about five times earnings.

It called that too pessimistic, noting that S&P forecasts output of light vehicles with combustion engines will decline by only about 0.2% a year over 2028-33 as hybrid growth offsets falling pure-combustion volumes.

France and Germany have proposed more flexibility on EU emissions targets for 2030 and 2035, which could give combustion-engine and hybrid vehicles a larger role beyond 2035. Citi said that could extend earnings at the Clean Air division, which accounts for 83% of group operating profit.

Marqeta, Coinbase to Bring Stablecoin-Backed Cards to Businesses

Cloud-based card issuing platform Marqeta (NASDAQ: $MQ) and major crypto exchange Coinbase (NASDAQ: $COIN) have expanded their partnership to help businesses offer payment cards funded by stablecoin balances.

Under the agreement announced Friday, Coinbase will hold customers' stablecoin balances and handle conversions between digital assets and fiat currencies. Marqeta will provide card issuance and payment processing, while managing relationships with banks and card networks.

The partnership will also use Base, Coinbase's blockchain, for on-chain settlement, which the companies say will support fast, low-cost transactions.

More From Cryptoprowl:

Coinbase Targets Banks As Institutional Crypto Adoption Grows

Businesses using Marqeta's platform will be able to fund their card programs around the clock and offer cards to customers who want to spend stablecoins without first manually converting their holdings into traditional currency.

The companies said the cards will work at millions of merchants globally that accept card payments.

Marqeta already issues crypto-backed cards for Coinbase. The new arrangement will allow Marqeta to extend stablecoin-backed payment options to both cryptocurrency-focused businesses and companies outside the crypto industry.

"Coinbase is enabling businesses to move money with the speed and efficiency they require," Alec Lovett, Coinbase's head of infrastructure products, said in a statement.

Last month, Coinbase also expanded its partnership with Citi (NYSE: $C) to connect traditional banking services with stablecoin payments for businesses. Coinbase will handle stablecoin transactions and convert payments into fiat, with Citi settling the funds for merchants as the bank of record.

Prior to that, the exchange partnered with payments provider Moov to bring stablecoin payment services to more than 1,000 U.S. community banks and credit unions.

These come as part of Coinbase's push to expand its services for banks and traditional financial institutions as institutional adoption of Bitcoin (CRYPTO: $BTC) and other cryptocurrencies grows.

Coinbase shares are currently trading at around $183 apiece, largely flat today.

title: Six Flags Struggled Financially Before Parkgoer’s Tragic Death: Dropping Shares, Crippling Debt, More
detail:
Six Flags Struggled Financially Before Parkgoer’s Tragic Death: Dropping Shares, Crippling Debt, More
Dylan Stewart/Image of Sport/Newscom/The Mega Agency (2)
Olivia Bellusci
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 11:00 AM CDT 2 min read
FUN
C
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Six Flags has struggled financially for quite some time.

On Monday, October 12, a parkgoer in Georgia tragically fell out of a roller coaster and died. After the incident, the amusement park's shares fell to their lowest level since 2009 on Tuesday, CNN reported.

The outlet noted that Six Flags stock is worth just $10 a share, even less than in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. The company has been riddled with debt since completing an $8 billion merger with Cedar Fair in 2024, and has not had a profitable quarter since the summer of 2024. Shareholders have seen their stock lose more than 80 percent of its value.

Image of Sport/Newscom/The Mega Agency

The high cost of living has also not helped the parks as "Mounting inflationary pressure" from gas prices and high borrowing costs "can't help but weigh on the theme park customer," according to research from Citigroup cited by CNN.

Citi analysts revealed a 15 percent year-over-year dip in foot traffic at the parks from April to June. In that same quarter, Six Flags reported a $203 million net loss, far more than the nearly $100 million loss the year before. The company's income wasn't enough to balance out $102 million in debt payments, and it ended up selling seven parks to EPR Properties for $331 million before the 2026 summer season began.

Another hurdle for the company is lawsuits from safety issues. Last month, the park closed the X2 ride at its Magic Mountain park in Valencia, California, and is facing multiple lawsuits over the rollercoaster, which may affect its chances of securing insurance.

BILL GREENBLATT/UPI/Newscom/The Mega Agency

"Although the company carries liability insurance to cover possible incidents, coverage may not be adequate to cover liabilities (and) the company may not be able to obtain coverage at commercially reasonable rates," Six Flags wrote in its annual financial filing earlier this year, per CNN.

While the outlet reported that Wall Street analysts predict the company will return to profitability in the summer months when it shares its earnings in November, losses are expected for the rest of the year.

Key Points

Interested in Morgan Stanley? Here are five stocks we like better.

Morgan Stanley shares fell 2.7% on Oct. 14 despite beating Q3 earnings expectations, reflecting investor skepticism similar to that seen with Citigroup.

Record wealth management revenue of roughly $9 billion and over $230 billion in net new client assets supported the bull case for steady, fee-based growth.

Analysts including TD Cowen and UBS maintain price targets of $210 and $236, respectively, both above the stock's post-earnings price of around $180.

In what is shaping up to be a big week of bank earnings, Morgan Stanley (NYSE: MS) delivered its Q3 report on Oct. 14, comfortably beating analyst expectations on the headline numbers. However, as with Citigroup Inc. (NYSE: C) the day before, the market sold off the stock.

Morgan Stanley shares fell 2.7% in the Oct. 14 session, leaving them at around $180, where they had begun the year after a 20% slide from July's high. For a headline beat, that is a chilly reception, and it points to a familiar tension in how the major banks are being judged this quarter. Like many of its peers in recent days, Morgan Stanley's results looked strong on the surface, but the underlying fundamentals gave investors reason to pause.

→ Tesla Wants to Make Its Own Chips—What Could Go Wrong?

So just how good was the quarter beneath the headline, and what do the results say about where the stock goes next?

The Wealth Engine Did Its Job

The best of the quarter came from the part of Morgan Stanley that is supposed to be boring, and that may be the most reassuring thing in the whole report. Its wealth management arm pulled in record revenue of roughly $9 billion while gathering more than $230 billion of net new client money, much of it the fee-based flows that keep paying year after year.

→ AMD's Support Could Help Fermi Stock Overcome Its Biggest Hurdle

This is the heart of the bull case as we head into the final few months of the year. For a long time now, Morgan Stanley has been reshaping itself from being a cyclical trading house into a fee-driven wealth manager, and a quarter like this shows the strategy working. The more of its earnings that come from steady advisory and management fees, the less the wider business should be exposed to the market's changing moods.

A Beat That Leaned on Trading

Look closer, though, and the quarter was less tidy than the headline, or solid wealth management results, suggested. A big slice of the strength came from equities trading, a notoriously fickle business that happened to boom last quarter, while fixed-income trading slipped and investment-banking fees barely grew. While it feels good when it lands like this, the snag is that a trading boom is the least reliable kind of beat there is, and can't be trusted to repeat itself.
